extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, mathematicians, and cognitive scientists interested in visualization and diagrammatic reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the epistemic legitimacy and role of visual thinking (diagrams, figures, imagery) in mathematical discovery, proof, and understanding, including when visual elements can count as non-superfluous parts of proofs. The discussion covers formal diagrammatic systems, common errors, and empirical/historical approaches to studying practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of visual thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual thinking in mathematics is widespread; it also has diverse kinds and uses. Which of these uses is legitimate? What epistemic roles, if any, can visualization play in mathematics?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central philosophical question: determine whether visual thinking has epistemically significant uses. Consider roles in proof, discovery, and understanding. Historical attitudes (Kantian emphasis on intuition, later anti‑visualism by Pasch, Hilbert, Russell, and partial revival by late 20th century authors) provide context for assessing legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish a proof from a presentation of a proof
rubrics_metrics.description: We should distinguish between a proof and a presentation of a proof. A proof can be presented in different ways. How different can distinct presentations be and yet be presentations of the same proof?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether two presentations count as the same proof, consider more than the central idea: overall structure, sequence of steps, and cognitive processes matter. Individuation is context-sensitive; identical informational order (e.g. ink vs Braille) can still count as the same proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify diagrammatic thinking as replaceable, superfluous, or essential
rubrics_metrics.description: In thinking through a proof, a given part of the thinking is replaceable if some other kind of thinking could stand in its place; it is superfluous if its excision without replacement would still count as thinking through the same proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the tripartite taxonomy: (a) all diagrammatic thinking is superfluous; (b) some is non-superfluous but replaceable by non-diagrammatic thinking; (c) some is neither superfluous nor replaceable. The text argues (via formal examples) that (c) obtains: some diagrammatic thinking is essential and not replaceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reliability for visual thinking to contribute to proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The main objection to diagrammatic reasoning is that visual reasoning is unreliable and therefore cannot contribute to proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To permit diagrams as part of proofs, one must show their reliability (or at least non‑unreliability) in context. This can be done by demonstrating soundness of the representational/inferential apparatus (e.g. formal systems) or by other non‑visual demonstrations that validate diagrammatic steps. Consider both normative and empirical evidence of reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: A formal derivation alone is syntactic; proof requires interpretation and soundness
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal derivation on its own is a syntactic object but not a proof. Without an interpretation of the language of the formal system and a demonstration of the system's soundness with respect to that interpretation, one lacks reason to believe derived conclusions are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a diagrammatic formal system, require: (i) syntactic derivations (which may be diagrams), (ii) an interpretation mapping syntax to mathematical content, and (iii) a soundness proof connecting derivations to truths in the interpretation. Only derivation + interpretation + soundness proof constitute a proof of the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal diagrammatic systems must have demonstrated soundness to make visual thinking non-superfluous
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal system which has diagrams in place of formulas among its syntactic objects, and inference rules that operate on diagrams, can make diagrammatic thinking non-superfluous provided its soundness is shown relative to an interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nathaniel Miller's FG (a formal diagrammatic system of Euclidean geometry) and its derivation of the construction of an equilateral triangle. Use such formal demonstrations as paradigms showing that inspecting sequences of diagrams can legitimately count as thinking through a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'relevant mismatch' between diagrams and captions
rubrics_metrics.description: Error type (1): a diagram is unfaithful to the described construction—representing something with a property that is ruled out by the description, or lacking a property entailed by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: diagrams used in the 'all triangles are isosceles' argument misplace the intersection point inside when it must be outside (Rouse Ball). Such mismatches are comparatively rare and usually avoidable with care; assess fidelity of diagram to textual description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unwarranted generalization from diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Error type (2): drawing conclusions from features of a particular diagram that do not hold in the general case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about inferring general properties from a single or unrepresentative figure. Philosophical concern: diagrams can mislead when a pictured instance has accidental features; demand either formal justification or argument that rules out accidental artifacts of the drawing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware over-formalization that obscures intuitive understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: For most purposes there is no need to master a formal system; in a formalized version of a proof, the original intuitive line of thought is liable to be obscured by a multitude of minute steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating proofs, weigh the costs and benefits of formalizing diagrammatic reasoning: formal systems can model reasoning but may hide the central intuitive idea; prefer formalization only after careful study of practice and when it serves explanatory or reliability aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior empirical and historical investigation before formal modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Before developing formal systems that aim to model real mathematical reasoning with diagrams, more investigation of actual practice is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two recommended branches of investigation: (i) close historical study of practices (e.g. Manders on Euclid) and (ii) cognitive study of individuals' use of diagrams. Use results from these studies and from visual perception/imagery literature to inform formal modeling and normative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat visual representations as information-bearing and potentially deductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual representations, such as geometric diagrams, graphs, and maps, all carry information. Taking valid deductive reasoning to be the reliable extraction of information from information already obtained, representations composing a proof can be visual as well as linguistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework: if diagrams reliably encode information and there are reliable diagrammatic inference steps, then visual components can play the same epistemic role as sentential components. Consider heterogeneous systems (formulas + diagrams) and work assessing their metalogical properties (Barwise & Etchemendy, Shin, Hyperproof).
